findings.title: Permission denial cache locks in denies for 30s with no invalidation, defeating the new DB fallback for repeat checks
findings.body: In Check(), once a DB query confirms a deny, the result is written to permDenialCache (line 154) and every subsequent Check for the same (namespace, user, action, resource name, folder) returns deny from the denial cache before the permission cache or the database is ever consulted. This means the new 'requery the DB when cached permissions deny' fallback (the core fix of this PR) only ever runs once per resource: after the first denied check, a permission granted on that exact resource (e.g. an admin shares a dashboard with a user who was just denied, or a permission row commits shortly after a racing check during resource creation) is not honored for up to 30 seconds. There is also no invalidation hook: in the in-proc path the service uses a private LocalCache that Grafana's accesscontrol cache-invalidation on permission changes cannot reach, and in the shared-cache (RegisterRBACAuthZService) path a denial written by one instance blocks all instances. Consider not writing a denial entry when the deny could race with a grant/creation, or invalidating the denial key when a fresh DB query for the same user/action returns an allow (e.g. via a List or another resource's fallback).

findings.title: Denial-cache test does not actually verify the short-circuit and its comment contradicts its data
findings.body: In the 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' subtest, the comment says 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked', but the permCache entry is set to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} — i.e. a deny, not an allow. Because the value is false, and the default fakeStore in setupService returns no permissions, the test would pass even if the permDenialCache check in Check() were deleted entirely: the permCache deny would fall through to the DB path, which also returns deny. To actually prove the denial cache short-circuits, the permCache entry should be {"dashboards:uid:dash1": true} and the fake store should return that permission, so that only the denial entry can produce the expected false.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric now conflates denial-cache hits with permission-cache hits and mislabels decisive-but-denying hits as misses
findings.body: After this change a denial-cache hit increments permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (line 118), so a fast negative answer from the new permDenialCache is indistinguishable from a permission-cache allow in this metric. Conversely, when cached permissions are found but checkPermission denies and the request falls through to the DB, the code increments permissionCacheUsage with "false" (line 137) even though the permission cache was hit — a real hit is recorded as a miss. The metric can no longer be used to observe the new DB-fallback path or the denial-cache hit rate, which are exactly the behaviors this PR introduces and would want to monitor in production. Consider separate label values or a distinct metric for the denial cache and for 'cache hit but denied, fell back to DB'.

findings.title: In-proc authz client cache removal puts a gRPC call plus per-check JSON decode on every access check
findings.body: For the default (in-proc) mode the client is now built with a NoopCache, so every authorization check in Grafana core — which happens several times per HTTP request on the hottest path — performs an in-proc gRPC roundtrip, and on the server each cache hit requires JSON-unmarshaling the user's full permission scope map (cacheWrap uses encoding/json, and users with many scoped dashboard/folder permissions have large maps). The previous 30s client-side cache absorbed repeated identical checks entirely in memory. Removing it is necessary for the correctness fix (the client cache served stale denies for newly created resources), but a client-side cache that only caches positive responses would preserve most of the benefit without reintroducing the stale-deny bug, since denies would still always reach the server (where the new denial cache provides the fast negative path). Worth measuring the per-request overhead before merging, or implementing positive-only client caching.
